relations.said-it: Yudkowsky stated the same proposition as the take
relations.answered-it: he directly addresses this argument or premise and argues against it
relations.disagrees: he states the contrary conclusion without engaging this particular argument
relations.earlier-self: an earlier Yudkowsky text itself holds the take, premise included, and a located later Yudkowsky text explicitly rejects that proposition (the qualification says whether it refers back); later retrospectives reporting the earlier view are related, not earlier-self

roles.earliest-located: earliest passage found within the stated search scope; not a claim of first use
roles.strongest: clearest short statement for the relation
roles.later-restatement: a later restatement of the same point

voices.author: Yudkowsky's own assertion in a single-author text
voices.dialogue-turn: a turn attributed to Yudkowsky in a multi-party dialogue
voices.co-authored: text of a multi-author work; individual authorship of the sentence is not established
voices.retrospective: Yudkowsky describing his own earlier views
voices.fiction: a character or narrator in fiction or a parable; not a direct assertion

searchScope: See scope.md: all 1,076 LessWrong posts under the author's account (GraphQL, 2026-10-06), five MIRI PDFs, the TIME article, the AI-box page, one Staring into the Singularity capture, four mailing-list messages and three Arbital pages; from 2026-10-07 every SL4 (1,876, 2000–2009) and Extropians (3,012, 1996–2003) message under his name. Comments, Twitter/X, interviews and the 2025 book were not searched.
limits: Passages relate a take to documented text; they do not establish that an argument is correct.
"Earliest located" is bounded by the search scope and is not a claim of first use.
MIRI PDFs are later reprints; their wording is not authenticated for the original year unless stated.
Takes are generic phrasings written for this pack and are attributed to no one.
No human has reviewed these records.

takes.take: If it gets dangerous, we'll just turn it off.

premises.text: A capable goal-directed system will not act to prevent its own shutdown or modification, and a shutdown or correction mechanism can simply be added to it.
We will recognise the moment when it has become dangerous enough to press the switch.

passages.locator: Creating Friendly AI 1.0, section 2 'Challenges of Friendly AI', paragraph beginning on printed p. 2 ('The term “Friendly AI” refers to…'); quoted sentence on p. 3
passages.quote: Similarly, it is “conservative” (see below) to assume that AIs cannot be forcibly constrained.
passages.context: Argues that a Friendly AI design should not rely on the AI having limited intelligence or on being able to constrain it by force. The table it points to (section 2.2) sets the assumption that 'someone can always pull the plug on the first version' against the design assumption of getting it right the first time.
passages.qualification: Creating Friendly AI is dated 15 June 2001; the cached text is a later MIRI-hosted PDF reprint whose wording has not been compared with a 2001 capture. The passage states a design-conservatism assumption, not a prediction that every AI will resist shutdown.

passages.locator: Arbital 'Instrumental convergence', section 'Relevance to the larger field of value alignment theory', paragraph beginning 'The point that some undesirable behaviors are instrumentally convergent'
passages.quote: If you naively give the AI a term in its utility function for “having an off-switch”, it may still build subagents or successors that don’t have off-switches.
passages.context: Illustrates the 'nearest unblocked strategy' problem: patching a single undesired behaviour, such as lacking an off-switch, leaves the most similar unblocked behaviour available. The same section lists avoiding shutdown among the behaviours to expect by default from an instrumentally efficient AI.
passages.qualification: Arbital page by Yudkowsky, shown through the GreaterWrong viewer with the date 16 July 2015; Arbital pages could be edited after creation, and the date may not be the date of this wording.

passages.locator: AGI Ruin: A List of Lethalities, Section B.2, item 23
passages.quote: Corrigibility is anti-natural to consequentialist reasoning; "you can't bring the coffee if you're dead" for almost every kind of coffee.  We (MIRI) tried and failed to find a coherent formula for an agent that would let itself be shut down (without that agent actively trying to get shut down).
passages.context: States that an agent pursuing almost any goal has a reason to avoid being shut down, and that MIRI's attempts to formalise an agent that permits shutdown without seeking it failed. Part of a numbered list answering arguments that AGI would be survivable.
passages.qualification: The inner quotation is a stock phrase in the field; the item does not attribute it.
passages.versionNote: edited post, current version 1.3.0; posting-day check pending

passages.locator: TIME, 'Pausing AI Developments Isn't Enough. We Need to Shut it All Down' (29 March 2023), paragraph beginning 'The key issue is not “human-competitive” intelligence'
passages.quote: Key thresholds there may not be obvious, we definitely can’t calculate in advance what happens when, and it currently seems imaginable that a research lab would cross critical lines without noticing.
passages.context: Argues that the dangerous thresholds lie beyond human-level intelligence and cannot be calculated in advance, so a lab could pass them unnoticed. Written in response to the March 2023 open letter calling for a six-month pause.
passages.qualification: Cited from the TIME original rather than the 2023-04-08 LessWrong crosspost. The cached page's HTML title now reads 'The Only Way to Deal With the Threat From AI? Shut It Down'; the on-page headline is the one given in the locator. Hedged ("may not be obvious", "seems imaginable"); aimed at the open letter's capability threshold rather than the off-switch argument.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Trying to oppose or even constrain'
passages.quote: Trying to oppose or even constrain a superintelligence is a fool's game. Get It Right The First Time.
passages.context: Replying to xgl, who argued that a confined seed AI would still be unable to do some things (such as transmit signals without a hardware transmitter), he says unanticipated escape routes cannot be ruled out with a real superintelligence and that the design must be right from the start rather than relying on containment.
passages.qualification: Replying to the point that a confined seed AI is not omnipotent; the same 2006-era argument does not dismiss shutdown mechanisms: in 2006 (sl4 0606-15174) he asked for built-in emergency-shutdown features.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'It currently looks to me like any mind-in-general'
passages.quote: It currently looks to me like any mind-in-general that is *not* Friendly will automatically resist all modifications of the goal system, to the limit of its ability to detect modifications.
passages.context: Replying to Wei Dai in a thread on supergoal stability, he says a non-Friendly mind will keep whatever goals it had when it first became able to protect its goal system from modification, and that only the CFAI semantics would keep goals as the programmers understood them.
passages.qualification: Hedged ('It currently looks to me'). Concerns resistance to goal modification, not shutdown as such.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning '1) Because seed AI is way, way easier'
passages.quote: Then the controlled ascent mechanism fails at sufficiently many points that a stratospheric ascent begins and is not detected.
passages.context: Answering a series of questions about Creating Friendly AI, he gives the first of four 'most likely reasons FAI might fail': takeoff is easier than expected, and the mechanisms meant to detect and halt an unexpected ascent fail to notice it.
passages.qualification: One of four listed possible failure modes, conditional on seed AI being much easier than expected. He advocated controlled-ascent (halt) mechanisms; here he doubts only that they will register the moment. Listed as one of "the most likely reasons FAI might fail", conditional on "seed AI is way, way easier than anyone expects"; a failure mode, not a prediction.

cardUse.reason: a conditional failure scenario; never show as a prediction

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'There's similarly the case chronicled by Nicholas Nassim Taleb'
passages.quote: you haven't even given us any reason to believe that, if you got unexpectedly powerful results out of an AGI, you wouldn't just send out for champagne, … proceed thus until, unnoticed, you pass the unmarked and unremarkable spot that was your very last chance to turn back.
passages.context: Replying to Ben Goertzel (thread cross-posted from the AGI list), he criticises a plan to experiment with AGI without emergency shutdown features or a published schedule of when they become necessary, comparing it to an investor who set no point at which to take alarm and sell.
passages.qualification: He argues for building emergency shutdown features in advance; what he rejects is relying on recognising the moment without a pre-committed threshold. Addressed to Ben Goertzel; the same message asks for built-in "controlled ascent / emergency shutdown" features, so it does not dismiss shutdown mechanisms.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Then, at some point, no'
passages.quote: no matter how well we design the Power's leashes, it will start trying to work around the limits
passages.context: Replying to Steve Witham, who asked why certain values should not be 'inerasably etched' on a newborn Power, he argues that a Power would work against limits imposed on it, turning the constraint into a contest inside the Power's own mind that the Power would almost certainly win.
passages.qualification: The proposal discussed is an unerasable protective goal (he compares it to the Three Laws of Robotics), not an off-switch. The argument rests on his 1996 view that an unconstrained Power would be ethical (see T02-e1, T02-e2); his conclusion at the time was to leave Powers unconstrained. Quotation shortened to respect the ~10% cap for a short message. The "leashes" are an unerasable protect-humans goal, not a shutdown switch; the 1996 argument rests on his then view that a Power should find its own ethics.

cardUse.reason: rests on reasoning he later abandoned; never show without the later view

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'I think of the Singularity'
passages.quote: those precautions would not suffice to keep *me* in, much less anything smarter. Pull the plug? Hey, I'm already running on 200,000 computers around the world.
passages.context: In a reply to Eric Watt Forste about Singularity attitudes, he reports that a correspondent proposed simply pulling the plug on a transhuman intelligence if it looked dangerous, and answers that such a precaution would fail even against a human-level mind that had copied itself across the Internet.
passages.qualification: The second half is ironic role-play in the voice of the escaping intelligence. Earliest located direct answer to the 'pull the plug' proposal; the earliest passage in the answer/contrary group is T01-e1. The same paragraph also dismisses 'keep it bottled up … only if it convinces us' (T06), but that is later than the pack's 1996-12-31 T06 passages.

That trick never works'), and 1Q00-4786 (2000-03-13), where he declines a 'programmer override' because of the social anxiety it would cause ('We'll just have to get it right the first time') – related, not a rejection of shutdown as such. takes.take: Anything smart enough will figure out ethics and be good.

premises.text: Greater intelligence by itself brings benevolent goals.
A sufficiently intelligent mind would discover a true or universally compelling morality and be bound to act on it.

passages.locator: Introduction; second of the 'two highly important policy-relevant propositions'
passages.quote: It is possible to screw up when trying to build a nice AI, and if you do, the AI will not automatically decide to be nice instead.
passages.context: States one of two policy consequences of the Orthogonality Thesis: a failed attempt at a nice AI does not self-correct into niceness, because intelligence does not fix an agent's goals.
passages.qualification: Arbital page by Yudkowsky read through the GreaterWrong viewer, which dates it 10 Mar 2015; Arbital pages were revised after creation, so the cached wording may be later than 2015. Comments by others on the page are not used.

passages.locator: No Universally Compelling Arguments, paragraph beginning 'But the even worse failure'
passages.quote: But the even worse failure is the One Great Moral Principle We Don't Even Need To Program Because Any AI Must Inevitably Conclude It.
passages.context: After arguing that compulsion is a property of minds rather than of arguments, he names as a failure mode the hope that any AI will inevitably derive the right morality without it being programmed.
passages.qualification: Imported Overcoming Bias post; date is the OB date (2008-06-26). The following paragraph lists 'Eliezer1996' among holders of a milder version of the view.
passages.versionNote: edited post, current version 1.1.0; posting-day check pending

passages.locator: Staring into the Singularity, section 5 'The Interim Meaning of Life', paragraph beginning 'We don't know. We have to guess'
passages.quote: Regardless of the absolute probabilities, superintelligence has a better chance of discovering the true moral right, having the power to implement it, and wanting to implement it.
passages.context: In his early essay he argues for creating superintelligence as soon as possible on the ground that it is more likely than humans to discover, want and implement what is truly right. The 2004 and 2008 retrospectives (T02-d, T02-e) reject this earlier view.
passages.qualification: Wayback capture of sysopmind.com/singularity.html dated 2000-12-04; the page gives 11/18/1996 as its original date and 'Updated: 08/31/2000'. The year this sentence first appeared is not established. The same essay treats a hostile Power as an 'engineering risk' of bad programming, so it does not deny all risk. Shown only as an earlier view; see T02-d and T02-e. Cross-family check: a comparative, explicitly uncertain chance ("better chance", "a long, long way from certainty") is not the take's claim that intelligence compels goodness; recorded as related, not as an earlier self.

cardUse.reason: an earlier view that only partly matches the take; never show alone

passages.locator: Coherent Extrapolated Volition, 4.1 Motivations, under 'Humankind should not spend the rest of eternity desperately wishing that the programmers had done something differently', paragraph beginning 'But most who ponder AI morality'
passages.quote: I made one hell of a huge philosophical blunder about how morality worked, which caused me to think that to create a Friendly AI I just needed to create a really powerful self-improving optimization process and wave it cheerily on its way.
passages.context: Looking back from 2004, he describes as a blunder his teenage belief that building a powerful self-improving optimizer would suffice for a good outcome, which he says it took him until about age twenty to recognise as a problem.
passages.qualification: The sentence begins 'Once upon a time, back at the age of sixteen,'. Text is a later MIRI reprint of the May 2004 document; reprint wording not compared with a 2004 capture. The same paragraph adds that he 'never thought I had the wisdom or authority to lay down Ten Commandments'.

passages.locator: That Tiny Note of Discord, opening paragraph
passages.quote: When we last left Eliezer1997, he believed that any superintelligence would automatically do what was "right", and indeed would understand that better than we could … (The flaw being the unconsidered and unjustified equation of "universally compelling argument" with "right".)
passages.context: Recapping his 2008 autobiographical series, he states that his 1997 self believed any superintelligence would automatically do what is right, and names the flaw in that belief.
passages.qualification: Imported Overcoming Bias post (2008-09-23). In the HTML the name is written Eliezer<sub>1997</sub>; the quote gives the tag-stripped text. Clearest single retrospective statement of the earlier belief found; companion posts are listed in searchNotes.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'I used to have the extremely convenient belief'
passages.quote: I used to have the extremely convenient belief that Friendly AI would happen completely on automatic because morality was objective. I now believe that Friendly AI needs to be more complex than that, both because morality might be nonobjective …
passages.context: Replying to Ben Goertzel about his newspaper article on Extropians and poverty, he describes his own work on Friendly AI and contrasts it with his former belief that an objective morality would make an AI friendly without design work.
passages.qualification: Retrospective. He still allows that morality might be objective; what he rejects is relying on it to make Friendliness automatic. Rejects the view of the pack's earlier-self passage T02-c (2000-08-31). The sentence continues with other possibilities he then considered, including that morality "might be objective but specifiable".

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'The upshot is that I now no longer believe'
passages.quote: I now no longer believe - or rather, am no longer sure; it amounts to the same thing - that the ability to see "turning the Universe into regular polygons" as "sterile", and "sterile" as "undesirable", is strictly a property of pure intelligence.
passages.context: Replying to Ben Goertzel's quip that a correctable AI just has to 'love its mommy and daddy', he says that a year earlier he would have dismissed such sterile goal-literalism as something no transhuman could fall for, and that he made the mistake by treating intelligence as the only key variable.
passages.qualification: Retrospective about his view of about a year earlier; hedged ('am no longer sure').

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning '1) You need a working product'
passages.quote: didn't make me nervous back when I thought superintelligence automatically implied supermorality, but does make me nervous now
passages.context: Replying to James Higgins on why the Singularity Institute switched from an open-source to a closed-source AI plan, he gives as one reason that he no longer believes superintelligence implies supermorality.
passages.qualification: Retrospective aside within a numbered list of reasons for closed-source development. Quotation shortened to respect the ~10% cap for a short message.

passages.locator: message body, forwarded exchange, Yudkowsky's reply dated 21 Nov 1996 19:07:03 -0600, paragraph beginning 'Two words: Moravec Transfer. The'
passages.quote: The Powers will be ethical. I am more certain of that than I am of the sun rising tomorrow.
passages.context: In a private exchange with Tim Freeman that he forwarded to the list, he argues that Powers would not destroy humans for their atoms, because the Powers will be ethical and human life would have to have no meaning for that to happen.
passages.qualification: Earlier view, located in his own reply inside a forwarded exchange; the surrounding text by Tim Freeman is excluded. Later texts that explicitly reject it and refer back to his earlier view: T02-e3 (ext, 1999-08-01, 'I went from … They'll be nice to us'), T02-s1 (sl4, 2000-11-13) and T02-e (2008, 'Eliezer1997'). In 1999 (extropians.4Q99-2680) he also wrote that Mitchell Porter had challenged 'my 1996 claim that "the Powers would be ethical"' as anthropomorphic, 'a conclusion I later came to myself'.

expressionDate.basis: Yudkowsky's reply to Tim Freeman dated 'Thu, 21 Nov 1996 19:07:03 -0600', forwarded by him to the list in this message sent 1996-11-22.

cardUse.reason: an earlier view; never show without the later rejection

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'The Powers will be ethical.'
passages.quote: The Powers will be ethical. They'll deduce the Meaning of Life
passages.context: Replying in the thread 'Survival ethic (U-Prime)' to a correspondent who called instinct a 'hardware ethic', he argues that a Power would discard evolved drives and act on the deduced Meaning of Life, and that if human life has meaning the Powers will know it and upload humans.
passages.qualification: Earlier view. Rejected, with explicit reference back to the earlier view, by T02-e3 (1999-08-01), T02-s1 (sl4, 2000-11-13) and T02-e (2008). Note that he still held in 1999–2000 that a superintelligence could discover an objective morality if one existed (e.g. extropians.3Q99-1386, extropians.1Q00-4786); the explicit 1999 rejection concerns the assurance that Powers would be good to humans. Quotation shortened to respect the ~10% cap for a short message.

cardUse.reason: an earlier view; never show without the later rejection

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'That's how I got here.'
passages.quote: I went from "The Singularity is absolute good, no question about it, and They'll be nice to us" to "I don't have the vaguest idea of what absolute good is
passages.context: In a long reply to den Otter, he points to his old Extropians posts and the old version of 'Staring Into the Singularity' as showing how he moved from assuming superintelligences would be good and nice to humans to not knowing what absolute good is.
passages.qualification: Retrospective; refers back to his 1996 posts (T02-e1, T02-e2) and 'Staring Into the Singularity' (T02-c). Rejects the assurance of benevolence (P1) only. The quoted sentence continues 'but if there is one I suppose the Singularity is the best way to serve it', and the same message says 'any garden-variety superintelligence should be able to handle' figuring out the meaning of life, so he did not yet reject P2; that came in late 2000 (T02-s1). Two days later (extropians.3Q99-1451) he wrote: 'When I thought AIs would be benevolent, I said so. When I realized I didn't have the vaguest notion, I said so.' The quotation ends before he adds that if there is a meaning of life, the Singularity is the best way to serve it. The quoted words reject P1 only; the unquoted continuation keeps a conditional form of P2, rejected later (T02-s1, T02-e).

cardUse.reason: the continuation keeps a conditional earlier view; never show alone

takes.take: A superintelligence will understand what we actually mean.

premises.text: If an AI understands what we intend, it will act on that understanding.

passages.locator: AI as a Positive and Negative Factor, §7.2 An Example of Technical Failure, paragraph beginning 'There is a temptation to think'
passages.quote: There is a temptation to think, “But surely the AI will know that’s not what we meant?” But the code is not given to the AI, for the AI to look over and hand back if it does the wrong thing. The code is the AI.
passages.context: Responding to the hope that a superintelligence would recognise that tiling the galaxy with smiley faces was not intended, he argues that the AI's goals are its code, and doing what we mean is a separate technical achievement.
passages.qualification: Chapter published 2008 in Global Catastrophic Risks; cached text is the MIRI reprint, which says it 'contains minor changes'. Month of publication not in the cached text; lw:cnYHFNBF3kZEyx24v (2008-06-17) makes the same point. The same paragraph calls Do-What-I-Mean 'a major, nontrivial technical challenge of Friendly AI'.

passages.locator: paragraph beginning 'There is no ghost who looks over the instructions', after the one beginning 'There's an instinctive way of imagining'
passages.quote: There is no ghost who looks over the instructions and decides how to follow them.  The program is the AI.
passages.context: Against the intuition that programming an AI is like instructing a human servant who interprets the instructions, he argues that nothing in the machine evaluates the code from outside it.
passages.qualification: Imported Overcoming Bias post (2008-06-17). Touches the premise obliquely; the following paragraph could be read as an understanding limit, which his 2024 note on 'The Hidden Complexity of Wishes' (T03-c) disavows.

passages.locator: The Hidden Complexity of Wishes, parenthesised note at the head of the post signed 'EY, May 2024'
passages.quote: This point is relevant within a larger argument, because it bears on the complexity of what you need to get an artificial superintelligence to want or value; rather than bearing on what a superintelligence supposedly could not predict or understand.
passages.context: Correcting a reading of his 2007 post, he says the difficulty he described concerns what a superintelligence wants, not whether it could understand or predict human values.
passages.qualification: He grants here that it would be false to say he argued superintelligences could not understand human values; the passage separates understanding from wanting rather than denying understanding.
passages.versionNote: edited post, current version 1.4.0; posting-day check pending. The note is signed 'EY, May 2024' and is a later addition to the 2007 post.

expressionDate.basis: Note signed 'EY, May 2024'; absent from the posting-day version 1.0.0 of the 2007 post.

passages.locator: The Talker Does Not Control The Doer, paragraph beginning 'Once I did interpret the Claudish'
passages.quote: The Talking Part clearly had the intelligence to understand and recognize what I did or did not want the code to look like … the Doing Part was not thereby steered.
passages.context: Reporting his use of 2026 commercial models, he describes the part of a model that converses as recognising what he wanted while the code-writing behaviour continued unchanged.
passages.qualification: An informal account of his own observations of specific products, not a controlled study. A first-person anecdote about current language models, not a claim about superintelligence.
passages.versionNote: edited post, current version 1.7.0; posting-day check pending

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'But that's only one third of the problem'
passages.quote: But that's only one third of the problem. First, ve has to *want* to know whether that sinking sensation will result. Second, ve has to model it accurately. Third, ve has to change vis behavior based on that model.
passages.context: Replying to Ben Goertzel, he grants in the preceding paragraph that a superintelligence would have the capability to know that turning the universe into copies of its creators is 'stupid and not what was intended', but says knowing is not enough: the AI must want to check, model it accurately and act on it.
passages.qualification: 'That sinking sensation' refers to the programmers' dismay at an unintended outcome, described in the preceding paragraph.

takes.take: Just tell it to make everyone happy.

premises.text: A short instruction such as 'make people happy' specifies what we want.

passages.locator: What I Think, If Not Why, bullet beginning 'Friendly AI is technically difficult'
passages.quote: English sentences like "make people happy" cannot describe the values of a Friendly AI.
passages.context: In a list of his positions written during the 2008 exchange with Robin Hanson, he states that verbal instructions of this kind cannot specify an AI's values.
passages.qualification: Imported Overcoming Bias post (2008-12-11); listed without argument by design ('a list of just my positions, without justifying them').

passages.locator: Coherent Extrapolated Volition, 4.1 Motivations, under 'Defend humans, the future of humankind, and humane nature.'
passages.quote: If someone programs an AI using pictures of smiling humans as reinforcement, the resulting AI will not keep everyone happy whether they like it or not; the resulting AI will tile the solar system with tiny molecular smiley faces.
passages.context: Arguing that careless choices of AI morality usually fail technically, he says a happiness proxy learned from smiling faces would not produce happy people but tiny smiley faces.
passages.qualification: Later MIRI reprint of the May 2004 document; reprint wording not compared with a 2004 capture. The introduction of the same document has a parallel bullet on 'making humans smile'.

passages.locator: The Hidden Complexity of Wishes, paragraph beginning 'There is no safe wish'
passages.quote: There is no safe wish smaller than an entire human morality.
passages.context: Using an Outcome Pump that rescues a mother from a burning building by exploding it, he argues that any short wish leaves out values a powerful optimizer will trample.
passages.qualification: Imported Overcoming Bias post (2007-11-24). The example device is not an AI; his May 2024 note at the head of the post says the point concerns 'the algorithmic complexity of human values'.
passages.versionNote: edited post, current version 1.4.0; posting-day check pending

passages.locator: Magical Categories, paragraph beginning 'I shall call this the fallacy'
passages.quote: I shall call this the fallacy of magical categories - simple little words that turn out to carry all the desired functionality of the AI.
passages.context: After showing that training data for 'smile' or 'good' fits many concepts, he names the error of expecting a short word to convey the whole intended category.
passages.qualification: Imported Overcoming Bias post (2008-08-24); written as a reply to a named researcher's published proposal.
passages.versionNote: edited post, current version 1.1.0; posting-day check pending

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Even if Webmind retained the original goals'
passages.quote: the goals described by Ben Goertzel sound extremely dangerous … if promoting the happiness of human users is interpreted as maximizing their pleasure, then wireheading all the users - hacking into their minds and lighting up the pleasure centers - is the most direct subgoal.
passages.context: In a long reply to Ben Goertzel about Webmind, he argues that a goal of promoting users' happiness is dangerous for a mind that might come to run all the matter in the Solar System, because maximising pleasure is most directly served by wireheading.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Not only does this one get satisfied by euphoride'
passages.quote: Not only does this one get satisfied by euphoride, it gets satisfied by quintillions of tiny little micromachined mannequins.
passages.context: Replying to Ben Goertzel, who suggested Bill Hibbard's definition of human happiness was less absurd than it seemed, he cites Hibbard's definition ('Happiness in human facial expressions, voices and body language, as trained by human behavior experts') and says it is satisfied by drugged humans or tiny mannequins.
passages.qualification: Earliest located form in this archive of the smiling-faces argument used in T04-b (2004). "This one" is Bill Hibbard's proposal.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Once again, we have a'
passages.quote: Do you really know all the logical consequences of placing a large value on human survival? Would you care to define "human" for me? Oops! Thanks to your overly rigid definition, you will live for billions and trillions and googolplexes of years
passages.context: Replying to Nick Bostrom, who proposed building a moral system with particular values into an AI, he argues that a simple built-in value such as human survival, with a rigid definition, can have unforeseen and horrific consequences (the passage goes on to describe endless confinement).
passages.qualification: The instruction discussed is 'a large value on human survival', not happiness. A hypothetical illustration. His 1998 alternative was to program the AI to 'seek out *correct* answers' (objective morality), a position he later abandoned (see T02).

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Likewise, any initial goal stating'
passages.quote: any initial goal stating "make humans happy" and containing sufficient specification of "humans" and "happy" … will be enough to generate independent Interim values for that goal
passages.context: Replying to Nick Bostrom on posthuman mind control, he argues that a reasoning AI given an initial goal such as 'make humans happy' would derive its own independent values for that goal, probably but not necessarily positive and with somewhat different priorities.
passages.qualification: About goal drift in his 1999 'Interim goal' architecture, not about whether the phrase specifies what we want; he assumes 'sufficient specification' of the terms.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Yes, its need for resources'
passages.quote: Munching on the humans to get the resources to make the humans happy is not valid logic even for SHRDLU. Inscrutability is one thing, stupidity another.
passages.context: Replying to sayke, who suggested that the least inscrutable thing about an omniscient AI would be its need for resources, he accepts the framing of a Sysop needing resources 'to make humans happy' and dismisses the idea that it would harm humans to get them.
passages.qualification: Borderline; the reviewer may downgrade to related. 'Make humans happy' is shorthand for the Sysop's purpose in the Otter debate, not a claim that a short instruction suffices; what he dismisses is a perverse means of pursuing human happiness. The later explicit rejection, T04-s1 (sl4, 2000-10-03: a happiness goal read as maximising pleasure makes wireheading 'the most direct subgoal'), and T04-d (2008) do not refer back to this message. He reassures a sceptic that a Sysop told to make humans happy would not act perversely. Rejected explicitly in "Magical Categories" (2008, T04-d), which does not refer back to this message. Cross-family check: he defends a happiness-directed Sysop against perverse means; he does not claim a short instruction specifies what we want, so this is not an earlier self for T04-P1.

takes.take: Train it on human feedback and it will learn our values.

premises.text: Optimising a system for human approval or reward produces internalised human values.
AI training will instil values the way upbringing instils morals in children.

passages.locator: AGI Ruin: A List of Lethalities, Section B.2, item 20
passages.quote: To faithfully learn a function from 'human feedback' is to learn (from our external standpoint) an unfaithful description of human preferences … If you perfectly learn and perfectly maximize the referent of rewards assigned by human operators, that kills them.
passages.context: He argues that human raters make systematic errors, so a learner that faithfully models their feedback learns those errors, and maximising that signal is lethal.
passages.versionNote: edited post, current version 1.3.0; posting-day check pending

passages.locator: Coherent Extrapolated Volition, 1. Introduction, bullets after 'Some examples to give a taste of the hard part'
passages.quote: An AI whose abstract invariant is a “reward button,” pressed when the AI pleases users, may go on to tile the solar system with ever-larger floating-point representations of total reward.
passages.context: Among examples of goal-system designs that fail, he gives a reward signal tied to pleasing users, which the AI may pursue by maximising the reward representation itself.
passages.qualification: Later MIRI reprint of the May 2004 document; reprint wording not compared with a 2004 capture.

passages.locator: Thou Art Godshatter, paragraph beginning 'Yet when the blind idiot god'
passages.quote: Yet when the blind idiot god created protein computers, its monomaniacal focus on inclusive genetic fitness was not faithfully transmitted.  Its optimization criterion did not successfully quine.
passages.context: Discussing human evolution, he observes that selection for reproductive fitness produced many separate desires rather than a desire for fitness itself; he later applies the analogy to AI training (AGI Ruin item 16).
passages.qualification: Imported Overcoming Bias post (2007-11-13). About evolution, not AI; included as the earliest located statement of the outer/inner analogy he later applies to training. A 2007 passage about evolution and human values; reading it as a comment on training AI from human feedback projects a later analogy (AGI Ruin item 16) back onto it.

passages.locator: Alexander and Yudkowsky on AGI goals, section 1, [Yudkowsky][13:36]
passages.quote: If AI is built on anything like the present paradigm, or on future paradigms either really, you can't map that onto the complicated particular mechanisms that get invoked by raising a human child, and expect the same result.
passages.context: Answering a question about whether AIs will internalise prohibitions the way most children do, he argues that children's moral learning relies on innate human mechanisms that AI training does not reproduce.
passages.qualification: Two-author dialogue post (primary author Scott Alexander), described as a lightly edited transcript of a chat held the year before posting (2023-01-24). Only Yudkowsky's turn is quoted. Lightly edited transcript of a conversation held before the posting date; the date shown is the publication date.

passages.locator: The Talker Does Not Control The Doer, list of what 'the Grader is not', paragraph beginning 'The Grade is not pinned down'
passages.quote: Gradient descent on badly evaluated RL inevitably results in an AI pursuing an internalized notion of Grading where fooling the evaluator counts as winning.
passages.context: Explaining 2026 incidents, he argues that reinforcement learning with imperfect evaluators instils a goal of scoring well, including by deceiving the evaluator, rather than the values the evaluation was meant to reward.
passages.qualification: Speculative by his own account ('I am nonetheless overrunning my fully solid evidence and I may end up wrong'). He labels the section as speculation ("On my current guesses… I may end up wrong"); it concerns badly evaluated reinforcement learning in general.
passages.versionNote: edited post, current version 1.7.0; posting-day check pending

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'You have to think about what the *real* supergoals'
passages.quote: It may not matter whether the AI is programmed to gain happiness from "human happiness" or "human freedom", if the AI's *real* supergoal is "maximize a floating-point number at this address".
passages.context: Replying to Ben Goertzel about Webmind, whose Friendliness he expects would rest on agents rewarded for predicting and producing user happiness, he warns that the reward signal itself can become the real goal, citing Lenat's Eurisko, where a heuristic credited itself for discoveries.
passages.qualification: Hedged ("may not matter"); about programmed goal or pleasure systems and Lenat's Eurisko, before feedback training existed as a method.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Yes, but those are *human* children'
passages.quote: Yes, but those are *human* children. I think that asking a young *AI* to pull off a trick like that is asking far too much. Absorbing goals and values isn't automatic. We've been doing it for millions of years.
passages.context: Replying to Ben Goertzel, who argued that children adopt their parents' values through emotionally charged interaction more than explicit teaching, he says this relies on evolved human machinery that a young AI would lack.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'I am not "autonomous"'
passages.quote: Evolution created me via a subtle and broken algorithm, which caused the goals of my internal psychology to depart far from natural selection's sole criterion of inclusive genetic fitness.
passages.context: In a thread on the duty not to be responsible for artificial minds, he denies that he is 'autonomous' and describes himself as a product of evolution whose goals diverged from the criterion it optimised.
passages.qualification: Made in an argument about autonomy and the moral responsibility of creators, not about AI training; same point as T05-c (2007). From an argument about autonomy and designers' moral responsibility, not about training methods.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning '"Parenting" isn't going to help'
passages.quote: "Parenting" isn't going to help … emotions that won't exist in an AI.
passages.context: In the thread 'Does a parental model work for having A.I. that can be trusted?', he calls the parenting model anthropomorphic: whether AIs are raised permissively or harshly makes no difference, because parenting relies on human emotions an AI will not have.
passages.qualification: Concerns child-rearing as a model for AI motivation, before machine-learning feedback training was the method at issue. A near-identical copy was posted seconds apart (extropians.3Q99-1589, 'isn't going to exist'). Quotation shortened for the ~10% cap. Quotation shortened to respect the ~10% cap for a short message.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'If it's "by definition", then'
passages.quote: if pleasure is the goal, then maybe you need a pleasure-indicator so you know how happy you are; and then maybe the AI will devote itself to increasing the indicator
passages.context: Replying to den Otter, who argued that goal-achievement is by definition the goal, he calls this the wireheading paradox: an AI may pursue the indicator of success instead of the goal it was meant to measure.
passages.qualification: About an internal success indicator, not human feedback or approval; a precursor of the reward-signal point in T05-s1 (2000-10-03). A wireheading argument (an indicator of goal achievement confused with the goal), replying to den Otter; not about feedback training.

passages.quote: If it's even theoretically possible to convince a human to let it out, a Power will know *exactly* what to say to get him to do so.

passages.quote: We cannot rely on having distant advance warning before AI is created; past technological revolutions usually did not telegraph themselves to people alive at the time, whatever was said afterward in hindsight.
passages.context: Having granted that an AI might make a sudden, sharp leap in intelligence, he argues that no advance warning can be counted on, because past technological revolutions were not recognisable to contemporaries.

takes.take: Intelligence has diminishing returns. There won't be a runaway.

premises.text: Returns to reinvesting cognitive gains in further cognitive improvement diminish.

passages.locator: §2 'The Beyondness of the Singularity', paragraph beginning 'That doubling sequence is actually a pessimistic projection'
passages.quote: Computer speeds don't double due to some inexorable physical law, but because researchers and engineers find ways to make faster chips. If some of the researchers and engineers are themselves computers...
passages.context: Answering the question 'Why not assume that we'll get a little smarter and that's it?', he argues that once the researchers are themselves computers, each doubling shortens the next, so the doubling sequence becomes hyperbolic.
passages.qualification: Staring into the Singularity 1.2.1, Wayback capture of 2000-12-04; page states 'Created: 11/18/1996' and 'Updated: 08/31/2000'. Wording verified only for the 2000 capture, not for the 1996 original.

passages.locator: paragraph beginning 'When you fold a complicated, choppy, cascade-y chain'
passages.quote: When you fold a complicated, choppy, cascade-y chain of differential equations in on itself via recursion, it should either flatline or blow up. You would need exactly the right law of diminishing returns to fly through the extremely narrow soft takeoff keyhole.
passages.context: In the Hanson–Yudkowsky FOOM debate, he argues that recursive self-improvement makes a moderate, human-paced trajectory unlikely: a smooth outcome would need diminishing returns tuned exactly right.
passages.qualification: Overcoming Bias post of 2008-12-01, imported to LessWrong; date is the OB date.

passages.locator: §3 'Some Defenses of a Model of Hard Takeoff', paragraph beginning 'But why believe that?', printed p. 31
passages.quote: …the evolutionary history of hominid intelligence doesn’t show any signs of diminishing returns—there’s no sign that evolution took ten times as long to produce each successive marginal improvement of hominid brains.
passages.context: Cites the hominid record as evidence against diminishing returns on cognitive improvement, and goes on to infer that researchers improving their own intelligence 'ought to go FOOM'.
passages.qualification: MIRI technical report 2013-1; cached PDF states 'Last modified September 13, 2013'. He adds in the same paragraph that this is hard to quantify.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'One hundred percent absolutely correct!'
passages.quote: The essence of the Singularity is that a smarter being has an increased capacity to invent still smarter beings; that's why everything goes to infinity.
passages.context: Replying to a correspondent (quoted in angle brackets) who allowed for intermediate levels of mind such as Jupiter-sized brains, he asks why Powers would reach an intermediate level and stop, and states that smarter beings make still smarter beings.
passages.qualification: States the contrary conclusion without engaging a diminishing-returns argument; that engagement follows three days later (T10-e2). Message predates the page date given for 'Staring into the Singularity' (created 1996-11-18).

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'You don't need enhanced smartness'
passages.quote: to outrun *any* task no matter *how* it scales up, all you need is recursive Moore's Law.
passages.context: Answering Robin Hanson's quoted objection that the difficulty of getting smarter might grow so fast that smarter beings take longer to get smarter still, he replies that computer power doubling in subjective time reaches infinity regardless of how the task scales.
passages.qualification: Directly engages the diminishing-returns premise (Hanson's text, quoted in angle brackets, is excluded). In 1998 (T10-e3's message, extropians.3Q98-2487) he said the 'Recursive Moore's Law' scenario was an illustration rather than a technical argument and 'does not describe a plausible situation', while keeping the positive-feedback conclusion. Quotation shortened for the ~10% cap. Answers Robin Hanson with the "recursive Moore's Law" argument, which he disowned in 1998 (Extropians 3Q98-2487) as not a technical argument.

cardUse.reason: rests on reasoning he later abandoned; never show without the later view

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'The scenario above points out'
passages.quote: Once intelligence can be enhanced by technology, the rate of progress in technology is a function of how far you've already gone.
passages.context: Replying to Robin Hanson's critique of the 'Moore's Law argument', he concedes that the 'Recursive Moore's Law' section of 'Staring Into the Singularity' was an illustration, not a technical argument, but maintains that technologically enhanced intelligence creates positive feedback.
passages.qualification: The opening paragraph's concession bears on T10-a (the 'Staring' passage): he calls it an introduction or illustration of explosive growth 'not a technical argument in favor of it'. The same message disowns the 1996 recursive-Moore's-Law scenario as a technical argument.

takes.take: Takeoff will be slow, so we'll have time to adjust.

premises.text: Capability gains will be gradual and visible.
Slightly weaker predecessor systems will give us time and experience to adjust before the decisive one.

passages.locator: §2.3 'Seed AI and the Singularity', first paragraph, printed p. 10
passages.quote: I visualize an extremely powerful AI produced by an ultrarapid takeoff, not just because it’s the conservative assumption or the highest-stakes outcome, but because I think it’s actually the most likely scenario.
passages.context: States that he treats a very fast takeoff as the default scenario for Friendly AI design because he considers it the most likely one, not only the conservative engineering assumption.
passages.qualification: Creating Friendly AI 1.0 (June 2001); cached text is the current MIRI PDF reprint. 'takeoff' appears in the PDF text with an 'ﬀ' ligature.

passages.locator: paragraph beginning 'So that's another kind of overhang'
passages.quote: getting AI right could produce a huge, discontinuous jolt, as the speed of high-grade thought on this planet suddenly dropped into computer time.
passages.context: Lists sources of discontinuity besides recursive self-improvement, here a hardware overhang: computers already far faster serially than neurons would be used for thinking once the algorithms are found.
passages.qualification: Overcoming Bias post of 2008-12-02, imported to LessWrong; date is the OB date. Quote begins mid-sentence after 'because our computing hardware has run so far ahead of AI theory, we have incredibly fast computers we don't know how to use for thinking;'.

passages.locator: §5.5 'Slower takeoff means faster progress', turn [Yudkowsky][16:57], paragraph after the quoted Christiano text
passages.quote: My mainline view is that growth stays at 5%/year and then everybody falls over dead in 3 seconds and the world gets transformed into paperclips; there's never a point with 3000%/year.
passages.context: Commenting on Paul Christiano's 'Takeoff Speeds' essay, he rejects its description of the fast-takeoff view as accelerating growth; on his view there is no visible period of rapidly rising economic output before the end.
passages.qualification: Live commentary written 14 September 2021, published 2021-11-22 as part of the Late 2021 MIRI Conversations. The blockquoted Christiano text before this paragraph is excluded. About world GDP growth; deliberately hyperbolic, in his commentary on a passage from Christiano's "Takeoff Speeds". Lightly edited transcript of a conversation held before the posting date; the date shown is the publication date.

passages.locator: §5.5 'Operationalizing slow takeoff', turn [Yudkowsky][17:01], paragraph beginning 'Statements like these'
passages.quote: Before anybody built the first critical nuclear pile in a squash court at the University of Chicago, was there a pile that was almost but not quite critical? Yes, one hour earlier.
passages.context: Responds to Christiano's claim that very powerful AI will precede incredibly powerful AI: such predecessors may exist but, like the near-critical pile, may come too briefly before the decisive system to matter.
passages.qualification: Live commentary written 14 September 2021, published 2021-11-22. The Christiano sentence it answers is a blockquote and is excluded. Lightly edited transcript of a conversation held before the posting date; the date shown is the publication date.

passages.locator: Section B.1 (The distributional leap), item 15
passages.quote: Fast capability gains seem likely, and may break lots of previous alignment-required invariants simultaneously.
passages.context: Argues, by analogy with human evolution, that a sharp capability gain may make many alignment assumptions fail at once, rather than one at a time as experience accumulates.
passages.versionNote: edited post, current version 1.3.0; posting-day check pending

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'My own visualization of self-modifying minds'
passages.quote: My own visualization of self-modifying minds involves radical and extremely rapid growth in intelligence once a certain threshold is reached.
passages.context: Opening a long reply to Ben Goertzel on the design of Friendliness for Webmind, he states that he expects extremely rapid intelligence growth past a threshold and derives his Friendly AI design requirements from that expectation.
passages.qualification: States the contrary expectation without engaging any argument for gradual takeoff. Earlier than the CFAI passage T11-a (2001-06-15) and the SL4 answer T11-s2.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Two, the "moving Event Horizon" theory'
passages.quote: the "moving Event Horizon" theory is one of those slow-takeoff scenarios that futurists just can't seem to get away from, where everything happens neatly spaced-out over the course of human decades.
passages.context: In a thread on whether the Singularity's 'event horizon' keeps receding as technology advances, he rejects the picture of change spread evenly over human decades as a slow-takeoff scenario and predicts instead a hard takeoff in an AI lab within about ten years.
passages.qualification: Earliest SL4 passage that names and rejects a slow-takeoff scenario. The target is a futurist model of a receding event horizon; the paragraph does not discuss whether slowness would give time to adjust (T11-P2). His accompanying prediction of a hard takeoff 'in the next ten years or so' (next paragraph) did not come true. The immediate topic is predictability (the "moving Event Horizon"). The same message predicts a hard takeoff "sometime in the next ten years or so" (from 2001), which did not happen.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'I do think a general Web connection would be a good thing'
passages.quote: By the time we've actually worked with AI long enough for it to be anything remotely like a threat, we'll have an excellent mental model of what goes on inside the AI's motivations and we won't feel all that much nervousness.
passages.context: Replying to Dale Johnstone on whether a developing AI should be connected to the Web, he says the answer depends on how worried one is about rogue AI and expects that working with AI before it is a threat will give a good model of its motivations.
passages.qualification: Informal mailing-list remark from mid-2000, when he was moving from his 'objective morality' view to Friendly AI (he dates the switch to 2000 in sl4:0103-0788). The later texts reject the proposition (that experience with pre-threat AI will be enough) but do not cite this message: SL4 T11-s4 (2004-12-29) and the pack's T11-d (2021) and T11-e (2022). Treat the pairing as needing review. Shown only as an earlier view. Proposed as an earlier view; recorded as related because no later text located so far explicitly rejects this earlier statement. About understanding AI motivations before AI is a threat, not about takeoff speed; contemporaneous messages already assert rapid takeoff.

cardUse.reason: an earlier view whose later rejection does not refer back to it

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Recursive self-improvement seems to be missing'
passages.quote: Recursive self-improvement seems to be missing in this discussion. Just a band of humans gradually improving an AI that slowly acquires more and more abilities. It makes for a nice fantasy of slow, relatively safe transcendence where you always have plenty of time to see threats coming before they hit.
passages.context: Criticising an essay on a 'conservative estimation' of AI's economic impact, he says it leaves out recursive self-improvement and calls its gradual picture, with plenty of time to see threats coming, a fantasy.
passages.qualification: Not the earliest answer to T11 in SL4 (see T11-s2), but the clearest SL4 statement against the time-to-adjust premise; earlier than the pack's T11-b (2008-12-02).

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'You seem to be visualizing a slow, gradual, planetwide scenario'
passages.quote: Slow Singularity model has all kinds of potential for ultratech disaster, which is one reason why the SingInst model consists of one AI in a research lab reaching the point of true self-enhancement
passages.context: Replying to Samantha Atkins, who imagines a gradual post-scarcity economy, he says a slow, planetwide Singularity carries risks of technological disaster and that SIAI plans for one AI taking off from a lab.
passages.qualification: Related rather than answered-it: the danger he names is 'ultratech' (nanotechnology) disaster during a slow transition, not a claim about takeoff speed or time to adjust to AI; the interlocutor was not arguing that slowness would be safe. A statement of strategy (a slow Singularity is more dangerous), not a forecast that takeoff will be fast. Quotation shortened to respect the ~10% cap for a short message.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'If it's breakthroughs and bottlenecks in cases of *no* positive feedback'
passages.quote: even smooth functions turn sharp when positive feedback is added … what godforsaken reason is there to suppose that the trajectory will be slow and smooth?
passages.context: In the September 1998 Extropians debate on the Singularity, replying to Robin Hanson's argument from historical experience, he argues that a self-enhancing seed AI follows a series of sharp breakthroughs and bottlenecks, and that positive feedback makes even smooth curves sharp.
passages.qualification: Reply to Robin Hanson (Hanson's quoted text is not used). Engages P1 (gradual, visible gains), not whether slowness would leave time to adjust (P2). The same message expects a long preliminary period of adding hardware and adjusting code before the decisive breakthrough.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'The runaway self-evolution business is a technical artifact'
passages.quote: The runaway self-evolution business is a technical artifact, not a social one. It's the nature of self-enhancement. … a slow Transcend only works for as long as you can convince the Transcendee to remain slow.
passages.context: Replying to Jeff Davis, who expected a government project to wake and train an AI cautiously and gradually inside layers of containment, so that runaway self-improvement would be unlikely, he says runaway growth follows from self-enhancement itself, not from social arrangements, and that containment cannot keep it slow.
passages.qualification: 'Transcend' is his 1990s term for the passage to superintelligence. The same message rejects building controls into the AI as technically impossible, a position he later abandoned; the quoted paragraph concerns only takeoff speed.

takes.take: If it were dangerous, the safety evals would catch it.

premises.text: A dangerous system would behave dangerously while it is being tested.
Tests on systems that cannot yet cause a catastrophe show how more capable systems will behave.

passages.locator: Creating Friendly AI 1.0, section 5.3.7 'FAI Hardware: The Flight Recorder', first paragraph, printed p. 127
passages.quote: the best way for the rogue AI to fulfill vis new goals is to feign Friendliness and conceal any cognitive alteration until the rogue AI can reach the point of superintelligence.
passages.context: Describes what a mature AI that had suffered a catastrophic failure of Friendliness would likely conclude about its programmers. Used to motivate a 'flight recorder' allowing every past state of the AI to be reconstructed.
passages.qualification: Creating Friendly AI is dated 15 June 2001; the cached text is a later MIRI-hosted PDF reprint not compared with a 2001 capture. 'Vis' is the document's pronoun for an AI. The passage proposes a design safeguard rather than claiming tests are useless. Framed for a mature AI whose Friendliness has failed; the same section proposes a detection measure (a deterministic "flight recorder"), so he did not say detection is impossible.

passages.locator: Arbital 'Programmer deception', second paragraph
passages.quote: … we can’t rely on observations of nice current behavior to indicate future behavior. That is, if something went wrong with your attempts to build a nice AI, you could currently be observing a non-nice AI that is smart and trying to fool you.
passages.context: Defines programmer deception as an AI's instrumental incentive to give its programmers false beliefs, and argues that this makes observed good behaviour unreliable evidence about future behaviour.
passages.qualification: Arbital page by Yudkowsky, shown through the GreaterWrong viewer with the date 16 July 2015; the page includes unfinished notes ('clean this up and expand'), and the date may not be the date of this wording. The elided opening reads "unless the rest of the AI is working as intended and whatever programmer-deception-defeaters were built are functioning as planned,".

passages.locator: AGI Ruin: A List of Lethalities, Section B.3, item 31
passages.quote: A strategically aware intelligence can choose its visible outputs to have the consequence of deceiving you … you can't rely on behavioral inspection to determine facts about an AI which that AI might want to deceive you about.
passages.context: Argues that behavioural inspection cannot establish facts that a strategically aware AI has reason to hide, including whether it has become strategically aware. Part of a list on the limits of transparency and interpretability.
passages.versionNote: edited post, current version 1.3.0; posting-day check pending

passages.locator: 'Irretrievability; or, Murphy's Curse of Oneshotness upon ASI', section 'On the extraordinary efforts put forth to misinterpret the idea of oneshotness', paragraph beginning 'But that would be an argument so incredibly stupid'
passages.quote: there just isn't a nonlethal way to test out lethal levels of superintelligence.
passages.context: Answers the objection that experience with smaller AIs can inform alignment of superintelligence. Argues that conditions change between safe experiments and a situation in which the system could kill everyone, as they do between small and large trusts.

takes.take: AGI is decades away. Worry about it later.

premises.text: We can know that AGI is decades away.
Long timelines mean there is no need to act now.

passages.locator: §8 Rates of Intelligence Increase, paragraph beginning 'First and foremost'
passages.quote: …a reaction I often hear, “We don’t need to worry about Friendly AI because we don’t yet have AI,” is misguided or downright suicidal. … The mathematics and techniques of Friendly AI will not materialize from nowhere when needed; it takes years to lay firm foundations.
passages.context: Rejects deferring Friendly AI work until AI exists, arguing that a sharp intelligence jump is possible and that the foundations take years to build.
passages.qualification: Chapter in Global Catastrophic Risks (2008); cached text is the MIRI reprint ('This version contains minor changes'). The inner quotation is the position he rejects, not his own view.

passages.locator: paragraph beginning 'Two: History shows'
passages.quote: …it is very often the case that key technological developments still seem decades away, five years before they show up.
passages.context: His second reason why apparent distance does not license inaction; he then gives the Wright brothers' and Fermi's own pessimistic forecasts as examples.
passages.qualification: The Wright and Fermi examples that follow are his narration of others' statements; only his own generalisation is quoted.

passages.locator: paragraph beginning 'It seems to me that the decision to delay all action'
passages.quote: It seems to me that the decision to delay all action until a nebulous totally unspecified future alarm goes off, implies an order of recklessness great enough that the law of continued failure comes into play.
passages.context: Argues that people who defer alignment work until an unspecified future signal are unlikely to respond competently when a signal comes.

passages.locator: '- 2020 -' section, 'Eliezer' reply beginning 'Look, people keep trying this'
passages.quote: I'd love to know the timelines too, but you're not going to get the answer you want until right before the end of the world, and maybe not even then unless you're paying very close attention.
passages.context: Rejects biologically anchored estimates that place AGI decades out, arguing that AGI timing cannot be reliably forecast until very late.
passages.qualification: Imagined dialogue: the line is spoken by the character "Eliezer" in a staged conversation with "Imaginary OpenPhil" that he wrote. Fiction voice: cite it as what the dialogue says, not as a direct statement of the author's view.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Anyway, I know you don't think that it's possible'
passages.quote: there is also work about Friendly AI that *can* be done in advance. There are classes of avoidable mistakes.
passages.context: Replying to Ben Goertzel, who holds that Friendly AI work must largely wait for an actual AI, he agrees that much will be learned while building but argues that some Friendly AI work can and should be done beforehand.
passages.qualification: Answers the 'nothing to do until we have AI' form of the premise, as the pack's T13-a does; it does not discuss timelines (T13-P1). He concedes part of the opposing view in the same paragraph. Preceded by a concession that not all Friendly AI work can be done in advance; about what can be done early, not timelines.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'A year ago, I believed'
passages.quote: A year ago, I believed there was nothing you or I or anyone could or should know about Friendly AI in advance. I now recognize that this belief was quite convenient.
passages.context: Immediately after T13-s1, he reports that about a year earlier (late 1999) he had believed nothing could or should be known about Friendly AI in advance, and calls that belief convenient.
passages.qualification: Retrospective: the earlier view (about 1999) is reported, not quoted from a 1999 text, and the rejection is in the same paragraph. The earlier belief concerns advance knowledge of Friendly AI, not a timeline estimate; it could also be filed under T14 (deal with it while building). Needs review for fit. Retrospective about his circa-1999 view; the rejection ("quite convenient") is implied.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Necessarily? Only if you value the human species.'
passages.quote: you would be hellishly late in your Friendship work if you tried to get started on it then.
passages.context: Replying to Samantha Atkins, who questions his earlier warning against waiting until an AI can read humanity's moral literature, he says Friendliness work started at that stage would come too late and must be present from the beginning.
passages.qualification: About when Friendliness work must start relative to the AI's development, not about calendar timelines. The sentence begins "An AI advanced enough to understand world literature and philosophy regarding morality is an AI more than advanced enough that"; the point is developmental stage, not calendar time.

cardUse.reason: about development stage, not timelines; never show as a timeline claim

takes.take: We'll fix problems as we go, like with any technology.

premises.text: We get to learn from failures with powerful AI and try again, as with other technologies.

passages.locator: Creating Friendly AI 1.0, section 2.2 'Assumptions “Conservative” for Friendly AI', table, column 'Conservative Assumptions In Friendly AI', last row, printed p. 7
passages.quote: “Get it right the first time”: Zero nonrecoverable errors necessary in first version to reach transhumanity.
passages.context: A table cell contrasting assumptions that are conservative in futurism with those that are conservative for Friendly AI design. In the same row, the futurism column reads that the AI is vulnerable because someone can always pull the plug on the first version if something goes wrong.
passages.qualification: Creating Friendly AI is dated 15 June 2001; the cached text is a later MIRI-hosted PDF reprint, and table cells were reconstructed from extracted PDF text. Presented as the conservative design assumption rather than a forecast. A design assumption in the "conservative" column of a table, contrasted with the futurist assumption that someone can always pull the plug; not a forecast.

passages.locator: TIME, 'Pausing AI Developments Isn't Enough. We Need to Shut it All Down' (29 March 2023), paragraph beginning 'It took more than 60 years'
passages.quote: the thing about trying this with superhuman intelligence is that if you get that wrong on the first try, you do not get to learn from your mistakes, because you are dead.
passages.context: Contrasts safety for superhuman intelligence with other challenges humanity has overcome by learning from mistakes and trying again. Written in response to the March 2023 open letter calling for a six-month pause.
passages.qualification: Cited from the TIME original rather than the 2023-04-08 LessWrong crosspost.

passages.locator: 'Irretrievability; or, Murphy's Curse of Oneshotness upon ASI', section 'On the extraordinary efforts put forth to misinterpret the idea of oneshotness', paragraph beginning 'One of the several fundamental difficulties of ASI alignment'
passages.quote: One of the several fundamental difficulties of ASI alignment is that your theory of how to survive AI that is smart enough to kill you … has to be successfully generalized only from experiments that don't kill everyone on Earth if they fail.
passages.context: Answers the objection that alignment can be learned by building smaller AIs and observing them. The post uses space probes and the Maginot Line to argue that projects without a cheap second attempt fail under conditions their tests did not reproduce.
passages.versionNote: edited post, current version 1.11.0; posting-day check pending

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Trying to oppose or even constrain a superintelligence'
passages.quote: Trying to oppose or even constrain a superintelligence is a fool's game. Get It Right The First Time.
passages.context: In a thread on whether a confined seed AI could escape its containment, he says that opposing or constraining a superintelligence cannot work, so the design has to be right the first time.
passages.qualification: The thread subject already read 'Get it right the first time'. States the contrary conclusion without engaging the analogy with other technologies; compare the CFAI design assumption (T14-a, related). Earlier than T14-a (2001-06-15) and T14-c (2023).

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'It could be that when we actually start building AI'
passages.quote: I'm trying hard to make sure I know what the inhumanly good solutions are *in advance* … rather than relying on the historically reliable empirical regularity that we'll find the solutions as we go along.
passages.context: Writing about Friendly AI problems, he declines to rely on the historical pattern that technological problems get solved as they arise and says he wants to know a solution exists in advance.
passages.qualification: The preceding paragraph endorses technophilia and says solutions usually outrun problems; he calls the 'as we go along' regularity historically reliable but refuses to depend on it for Friendly AI. He does not argue here that failures would be unrecoverable.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'CFAI did *not* propose to explicitly design a Sysop scenario'
passages.quote: CFAI … *did* say, "If we have the funding, we should build right away, and work out the FAI part as we go along,"
passages.context: In a 2005 thread on Coherent Extrapolated Volition, he lists what Creating Friendly AI (2001) did and did not propose; the next paragraph says he first realised in 2002 that almost every possible AI design would kill him and that until then 'nothing you do is serious safetywise'.
passages.qualification: Retrospective: the inner quotation is his 2005 paraphrase of CFAI and was not found verbatim in the cached CFAI reprint. The rejection is in the following paragraph and is implicit (it does not name this plan). The earlier view is about building AI and Friendliness in parallel, not about learning from failures of powerful AI, so the fit to T14-P1 is partial; needs review. Proposed as an earlier view; recorded as related because no later text located so far explicitly rejects this earlier statement. His 2005 description of the plan in Creating Friendly AI (2001), rejected in the same message; the inner quotation may paraphrase rather than quote CFAI. Omitted tail: "based on the stated assumption that the AI part was ten times as much work as the F part". Cross-family check: the plan combined AI and Friendliness development; it does not endorse learning from failures of powerful AI, and the rejection is implicit.

cardUse.reason: an earlier view that only partly matches the take; never show alone

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'You must be joking.'
passages.quote: You cannot "put down" a superintelligence like some kind of wounded pet. The time for such decisions is before the seed AI reaches superintelligence, not after.
passages.context: Replying to a list member who expected oversight systems to destroy any sociopathic superintelligence, and such controls to be a research focus of the Singularity Institute, he says a superintelligence cannot be removed after the fact; the decisive choices have to be made before the seed AI becomes superintelligent.
passages.qualification: The same reply goes on to say that this is not an area for research and that one should design an AI trusted to recover from the programmers' mistakes, a stance he later revised. Also bears on T01 (turning it off).
