takes.take: It's just a tool. It doesn't want anything.

premises.text: A system can be highly capable without having goals or optimising for outcomes.
A system that only outputs answers or plans, leaving humans to act on them, is safe.

passages.locator: 'The Rhythm of Disagreement', paragraph beginning 'Nick Bostrom, however, once asked'
passages.quote: The Oracle AI still needs an internal goal system to allocate computing resources efficiently, and it has to have a goal of answering questions and updating your mind, so it's not harmless unless it knows what side effects shouldn't happen.
passages.context: Recounts his answer to Nick Bostrom's question whether an AI that only answers questions could be built and asked about Friendly AI. Argues that such an AI still needs goals and is not simpler than a Friendly AI.
passages.qualification: Imported Overcoming Bias post dated 1 June 2008; it recounts an earlier conversation whose date is not given. The same post says he later kept revisiting Bostrom's Oracle idea and allowed that it might be a pragmatically safer starting point if built to full Friendly AI standards. Reports an argument he gave Bostrom; the same paragraph concedes that an Oracle AI built to full Friendly AI standards "could end up a pragmatically safer starting point".

cardUse.reason: the quote alone overstates his firmness

passages.locator: 'Dreams of Friendliness', paragraph beginning 'To which the reply is'
passages.quote: To which the reply is that the AI needs goals in order to decide how to think: that is, the AI has to act as a powerful optimization process in order to plan its acquisition of knowledge
passages.context: Answers the proposal, stated in the preceding paragraph, that a question-answering AI 'wouldn't need any goals at all'. Argues that producing superintelligent answers requires powerful optimisation.
passages.qualification: Imported Overcoming Bias post dated 31 August 2008.
passages.versionNote: edited post, current version 1.1.0; posting-day check pending

passages.locator: 'Reply to Holden on 'Tool AI'', section 2 'Yes, planning Oracles have hidden gotchas too', final paragraph
passages.quote: there's a gap between benevolent-sounding English and actually benevolent algorithms which is the source of difficulty in FAI.  "Just make suggestions - don't do anything!" is, in the end, just more English.
passages.context: Replies to Holden Karnofsky's 2012 proposal of 'tool AI' that displays plans instead of acting. Argues that specifying such a system formally reintroduces optimisation over the user and the world, with unintended consequences.
passages.qualification: The post states that Luke Muehlhauser and Carl Shulman contributed and that the final edit was Yudkowsky's.

passages.locator: 'Ngo and Yudkowsky on alignment difficulty', section 3.3 'Hypothetical-planning systems, nanosystems, and evolving generality', turn [Yudkowsky][13:03][13:11]
passages.quote: What the heck would it mean for a planning system to be non-consequentialist? You're asking for nonwet water! What's consequentialist isn't the system that does the work, it's the work you're trying to do!
passages.context: Answers Richard Ngo's question why a planning system could not be non-consequentialist about which plans it outputs. Argues that outputting plans that achieve outcomes is itself consequentialist work, whatever system performs it.
passages.qualification: Edited transcript of a 2021 Discord dialogue posted 15 November 2021 (co-authored post). In the turn the sentence is framed as 'My answer is, "…"'. Lightly edited transcript of a conversation held before the posting date; the date shown is the publication date. Answers Ngo's proposal of a planner that only outputs plans for humans to follow: producing plans that score high when followed is consequentialist work.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Q: "Can non-Friendly AI or toollike AI be built?"'
passages.quote: Q: "Can non-Friendly AI or toollike AI be built?" A: "Not safely."
passages.context: Replying to Ben Goertzel on military AI, he describes 'toollike' superintelligences structured around immediate instructions rather than supergoals (which could be told to kill every living thing in a country) and answers his own question whether such AI can be built safely.
passages.qualification: The Q/A is his own rhetorical device, not quoted from anyone. A bare conclusion; the argument is only implied by the earlier paragraph about instructing a toollike SI. Earlier than T15-a (2008-06-01).

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'I do have to point out one minor consequence'
passages.quote: It won't do anything at all, internally or externally - not if you've designed it properly, so that making any choice requires a goal.
passages.context: Rob Harris argued that an AI not programmed to want or need anything would do nothing spontaneously and so would be safe; he agrees that rebellion is an anthropomorphic stereotype but answers that such an AI would do nothing at all, since every choice requires a goal, so an AI needs at least one goal.
passages.qualification: He accepts Harris's point against anthropomorphism. The next paragraph wants the initial goal to be one the AI could have derived itself, part of his early objective-morality view (later abandoned; see T02). The argument that capable action requires goals recurs in T15-b (2008).

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'The vast majority of coding would occur easily'
passages.quote: it could be that … a "coding drone" would be (1) independently motivated and (2) rapidly self-enhancing to the point of Powerdom. I personally believe (1) and (2).
passages.context: Commenting on the 'Geniebusters' website's doubts that an automated coder could be built, he argues that even a domain-specific 'coding drone' would outprogram humans and might be independently motivated and rapidly self-enhancing, which he says he believes.
passages.qualification: States the contrary of P1 for one domain-specific system; does not discuss whether a system that only produces outputs would be safe (P2). Quotation shortened to respect the ~10% cap for a short message. The elided words are "coding is such a general task that"; "Powerdom" (inside the quotation) is his term for becoming a superintelligent Power.

takes.take: Just give it good human values.

premises.text: Human values can be written down or taught as a ready, compact specification.
Present-day or programmers' values are settled enough to fix permanently in an AI.

passages.locator: AGI Ruin: A List of Lethalities, Section B.2, item 24, second paragraph
passages.quote: It's not just non-hand-codable, it is unteachable on-the-first-try because the thing you are trying to teach is too weird and complicated.
passages.context: Discussing a CEV-style AI that wants exactly what we would want, he argues that what would have to be aligned is too complex to specify or teach on the first attempt.
passages.versionNote: edited post, current version 1.3.0; posting-day check pending

passages.locator: Coherent Extrapolated Volition, 4.1 Motivations, under 'Humankind should not spend the rest of eternity desperately wishing that the programmers had done something differently', paragraph beginning 'There are fundamental reasons'
passages.quote: There are fundamental reasons why Four Great Moral Principles or Ten Commandments or Three Laws of Robotics are wrong as a design principle. It is anthropomorphism.
passages.context: He argues that short lists of moral rules only work on minds that already share human psychology, and that an AI given them would lose everything the list leaves out.
passages.qualification: Later MIRI reprint of the May 2004 document; reprint wording not compared with a 2004 capture.

passages.locator: Value is Fragile, paragraph beginning 'Value isn't just complicated'
passages.quote: Value isn't just complicated, it's fragile.  There is more than one dimension of human value, where if just that one thing is lost, the Future becomes null.
passages.context: Using boredom and subjective experience as examples, he argues that a specification capturing almost all of human value can still yield a worthless future if one dimension is missing.
passages.qualification: Imported Overcoming Bias post (2009-01-29).

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'A decision to take action X is synonymous'
passages.quote: Hardcoded Asimov Laws or even hardcoded hierarchical goal systems are a pipe dream. … you can't just export your own personal philosophy into an AI's mind. Your own personal philosophy is not necessarily stable under changes of cognitive architecture or drastic power imbalances.
passages.context: Advising Ben Goertzel on Webmind's goal system, he argues that hardcoded rules and goals will not survive a self-modifying AI's redesigns and that a programmer's own philosophy cannot simply be transferred into an AI.
passages.qualification: Written while he was moving from 'objective morality' to Friendly AI; the reason given is instability under self-modification, not the later complexity-and-fragility-of-value argument (T16-a, T16-d). Earlier than T16-b (2004-05).

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Ben, what makes you think that you and I'
passages.quote: Ben, what makes you think that you and I, as we stand, right now, do not have equally awful moral errors embedded in our psyche? A couple of centuries ago a lot of people thought slavery was a good thing. That's why a Friendly AI's morals can't be frozen.
passages.context: In a thread on military Friendly AI, replying to Ben Goertzel, he argues that present-day researchers probably hold undiscovered moral errors, so an AI's morality must be able to outgrow its programmers' rather than be fixed.
passages.qualification: Earliest located for T16-P2 specifically; T16-s1 is the earliest SL4 answer to the take overall.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning '3) Programmer-independent morality'
passages.quote: 3) Programmer-independent morality (morality which does not contain quirks or errors which were unique to the particular human programmers) is a desirable property of a Sysop.
passages.context: Rephrasing a list of Ben Goertzel's points, he adds programmer-independent morality as a design goal for a Sysop superintelligence.
passages.qualification: A design desideratum, not an argument against fixing present values; in late 2000 'programmer independence' was tied to his earlier objective-morality model (see sl4:0103-0788). "Sysop" was his term at the time for a superintelligence administering the world; terse, without argument.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Nuclear war isn't worth mentioning.'
passages.quote: An attempt to imprint the Three Laws … probably would backfire HORRIBLY!
passages.context: Replying to a list member who proposed leaving certain values, such as the protection of humans, inerasably fixed in a newborn superintelligence, he calls this line of thought the greatest known danger to humanity and says such an imprint would probably backfire.

takes.take: A pause or some regulation will handle it.

premises.text: A short pause (for example six months) is enough.
Regulation that is national, partial or not universally enforced can stop dangerous development.
Law can prevent the danger (the part he states himself, as an enforced worldwide halt).

passages.locator: TIME, 29 March 2023, paragraph beginning 'Hearing this gave me a tiny flash of hope'
passages.quote: Anyone talking that sanely deserves to hear how bad the situation actually is, and not be told that a six-month moratorium is going to fix it.
passages.context: Responding to an open letter calling for a six-month pause on training systems more powerful than GPT-4, he argues that the letter asks for too little.
passages.qualification: The same article says the six-month moratorium "would be better than no moratorium" and that he respects its signatories; the disagreement is about sufficiency.

passages.locator: TIME, 29 March 2023, paragraph beginning 'The moratorium on new large training runs needs to be indefinite and worldwide'
passages.quote: The moratorium on new large training runs needs to be indefinite and worldwide. There can be no exceptions, including for governments or militaries.
passages.context: Setting out what he thinks would actually need to be done, he calls for an indefinite worldwide halt to large training runs, backed by multinational agreements.
passages.qualification: He states the regulatory proposition himself, in a much stronger form than the take: indefinite, worldwide, without exceptions and enforced. The said-it relation applies to the call for law only. Presented as what "would actually need to be done" to have a chance, not as something that will handle the problem.

passages.locator: Section 6.2.2 Relinquishment (−), printed p. 211
passages.quote: At most, the US, or even the US and most of the other nations of the world, might implement an overt policy against AI. … bringing AI into the reach first of noncompliant nations, then of noncompliant factions, then of a lone hacker in a basement
passages.context: Arguing against relinquishing AI, he says that a national or near-global policy would be bypassed as rising computing power brings AI within reach of noncompliant nations and factions.
passages.qualification: Creating Friendly AI (2001); cached text is the current MIRI PDF reprint, wording not compared with a 2001 capture. In this text he opposed both regulation and relinquishment and favoured accelerating Friendly AI (sections 6.2.1–6.3); his 2023 and 2026 texts call for an enforced worldwide ban instead. No located passage explicitly retracts the 2001 position, so the change is not recorded as earlier-self. In 2001 he argued relinquishment was impossible in principle. In 2008 ("Fighting a Rearguard Action Against the Truth") he criticised his 2001 self for rehearsing technophilic arguments against relinquishment, and in 2023 he called for an enforced international shutdown (T17-b). The noncompliant-nations point persists (T17-e).

passages.locator: paragraph beginning 'If an ASI ban is to accomplish anything at all'
passages.quote: If an ASI ban is to accomplish anything at all, it has to be effective everywhere.
passages.context: Replying to a proposed national ban on new datacenters, he argues that a superintelligence built in another country is equally dangerous, so a ban must be universal.

passages.locator: paragraph beginning 'Artificial superintelligence is the very archetype and posterchild'
passages.quote: Artificial superintelligence is the very archetype and posterchild of a problem that can only be solved with force that has the shape of law, as in state-backed universal conditional applications of force meant to be predictable and avoided.
passages.context: Arguing against calls for unlawful action, he says that only lawful, state-backed and universal force could stop superintelligence from being built.
passages.qualification: His ask is an enforced worldwide ban backed by law, not "some regulation".

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'No; I think it would slow down AI'
passages.quote: slow down AI long enough for military nanotechnology to be developed
passages.context: Asked by Arona Ndiaye whether a ban on technologies would stop a hacker somewhere from producing the first seed AI, he answers no: a ban would delay AI until military nanotechnology arrives or hand the lead to rogue states.
passages.qualification: As in CFAI (T17-c), he argues against bans from a pro-acceleration position; his 2023 view calls for an enforced, indefinite worldwide halt (T17-b), which is a different proposal from the partial ban discussed here. Earlier than T17-c (2001-06-15). Answering "Even assuming a ban of technologies?"; "it" is a ban. The next sentence adds that a ban favours rogue-state projects. Quotation shortened to respect the ~10% cap for a short message. Opposite reasons to his later view: in 2001 slowing AI was harmful because military nanotechnology and rogue states would come first; in 2023 a pause is insufficient because nothing short of a worldwide halt is enough.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Look, these forces are going to a particular place'
passages.quote: Think of the Singularity as this titanic, three-billion-ton truck heading for us. We can't stop it, but I suppose we could manage to get run over trying to slow it down.
passages.context: In the same reply to Nick Bostrom, who urged taking as many precautions as time allows before a Singularity, he says the forces driving toward it are too large to divert, so trying to slow it would only get us run over.
passages.qualification: Not about regulation as such. In 1998 he wanted the Singularity reached as fast as possible (T22). He later argues for an enforced, indefinite, worldwide halt (T17-b, T17-f): he keeps the view that partial measures fail but reverses the conclusion that stopping is impossible or undesirable. A 1998–99 argument against delay, made when he expected a superintelligence to converge on correct morality; his 2023 call for an enforced worldwide halt (T17-b) reverses it.

takes.take: Why would it bother with Earth? The universe is huge.

premises.text: A superintelligence would leave us a small share, because sparing Earth would cost it very little.
Humans could trade with a superintelligence for what we need.

passages.locator: section ii, paragraph beginning 'What it all adds up to'
passages.quote: …if there's a bunch of superintelligences running around and they don't care about you -- no, they will not spare just a little sunlight to keep Earth alive.
passages.context: Concludes his reply to the claim that, because the solar system is large, superintelligences will leave Earth alone: a tiny cost is still a cost to minds that do not value us.
passages.qualification: The LessWrong post says it was 'Crossposted from Twitter with Eliezer's permission'; the original Twitter date was not established here. Crossposted from Twitter; the Twitter original was not retrieved.

passages.quote: A simple rejoinder is that just because Bernard Arnault has $170 billion, does not mean that he'll give you $77.18.
passages.context: Answering the claim that a superintelligence would leave Earth alone because the Solar System is big, he argues by analogy that great wealth does not imply giving a small share to any particular party.

passages.context: Replies to the suggestion that humanity could trade with superintelligences for sunlight: Ricardo's law assumes each party's labour goes on existing and does not show that keeping humans is more profitable than using their share.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'The requirement that "Friendliness not be affected by radical power imbalances"'
passages.quote: Good behavior should not be a subgoal of avoiding retaliation, or of obtaining reciprocal good behavior … from other entities. … all possible information can be obtained by duplicating the thoughts independently. An SI does not need other entities.
passages.context: Advising Ben Goertzel against grounding an AI's good behaviour in game theory or exchange, he argues that a superintelligence with strong nanotechnology would gain nothing from reciprocity with others.
passages.qualification: Design advice on grounding Friendliness, not a reply to a stated 'we can trade with it' argument; the omitted middle sentence says such an AI could avoid all retaliation 'simply by killing everyone'. Earlier than T18-d (2024). Conditional on the AI having strong nanotechnology.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Ben, it is extremely unlikely that Powers'
passages.quote: extremely unlikely that Powers would attempt to exterminate us deliberately … indifference very probably equates to extermination.
passages.context: Replying to Ben Goertzel's low-confidence guess that superintelligent Powers might neither help nor attack humans, he says deliberate extermination is unlikely but indifference would probably amount to extermination.
passages.qualification: Goertzel's guess is visible only in part in the quoted lines (Powers not 'closely engaged with humans'); Eugen Leitl's argument he endorses is not in the cache. Also used for T19 (T19-s1). Quotation shortened to respect the ~10% cap for a short message.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'A comparative handful of improvements to underlying *generators*'
passages.quote: Ricardo's Law of Comparative Advantage does not extend to chimps. And chimps are our closest cousins! What about mice? What about lizards?
passages.context: Replying to Robin Hanson's comments on his draft chapters, he argues that between-species differences in brain circuitry exclude weaker minds from a knowledge economy, so that trade-based intuitions from human economies do not carry over.
passages.qualification: Related: the argument concerns growth and trade among AIs and the exclusion of chimpanzees from the human economy, not directly whether humans could trade with a superintelligence for survival; a precursor of the comparative-advantage rejoinder in T18-d (2024). Replying to Robin Hanson on trade and hard takeoff: differences in brain circuitry exclude chimpanzees from the human knowledge economy.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'No, it could also be necessary'
passages.quote: … necessary that the SIs don't have something *else* they want to do with atoms.
passages.context: In a thread on superintelligences and comparative advantage, Lee Daniel Crocker argued that superintelligences would keep humans if we produced something they valued slightly more than our atoms, such as entertainment; he replies that this also requires that they have no better use for the atoms, and that optimising minds could build more entertaining replacements for us.
passages.qualification: Speculative and partly joking register (the paragraph ends with a jest about replacement entertainers). His next paragraph considers it somewhat more likely, though still not likely, that superintelligences would keep humans to encourage other Singularities. Short message (137 words), so the quotation is limited to about 13 words.

passages.locator: message body, Yudkowsky's reply dated Fri, 22 Nov 1996 02:27:52 -0600 within the echoed exchange, paragraph beginning 'And why wouldn't they bother'
passages.quote: why wouldn't they bother to direct a fraction of a fraction of a subconscious sub-personality to put in the necessary effort?
passages.context: In a private exchange he posted to the list, Tim Freeman worried that people revived far in the future would be irrelevant; he replies that uploading would be followed by upgrading, that Powers would have ample computing room, and that helping humans would cost them only a tiny fraction of their attention.
passages.qualification: Rests on his 1996 conviction that Powers will be ethical (T02); the it-costs-them-almost-nothing step is the one T18 relies on, but the passage is about benevolent upgrading rather than leaving Earth alone, so the fit to P1 is partial. Cross-family check: benevolent uploading and upgrading is not leaving Earth a resource share; not an earlier self for T18-P1.

takes.take: It has no reason to hate us, so it won't hurt us.

premises.text: An AI would harm humans only out of hostility.

passages.locator: Instrumental convergence, list after 'This is relevant to some of the central background ideas in AGI alignment, because:', first item
passages.quote: A superintelligence can have a catastrophic impact on our world even if its utility function contains no overtly hostile terms. A paperclip maximizer doesn’t hate you, it just wants paperclips.
passages.context: He argues that strategies such as acquiring resources serve almost any goal, so an AI without hostile goals can still be catastrophic for humans.
passages.qualification: Arbital page by Yudkowsky read through the GreaterWrong viewer, which dates it 16 Jul 2015; Arbital pages were revised after creation, so the cached wording may be later. Comments by others are not used.

passages.locator: AI as a Positive and Negative Factor, §10 Threats and Promises, paragraph on an AI rearranging matter by its optimization target
passages.quote: The AI does not hate you, nor does it love you, but you are made out of atoms which it can use for something else.
passages.context: Describing a superintelligence reshaping matter for its own target, he says the result is fatal unless the AI specifically values people, without any hostility being involved.
passages.qualification: Chapter published 2008; cached text is the MIRI reprint ('contains minor changes'). Earliest within scope; lw:jq5WAQEboeufkxzsg (2008-12-23) has a variant.

passages.locator: Intelligence Explosion Microeconomics, §1.3 AI Preferences: A Brief Summary of Core Theses, Instrumental Convergence Thesis
passages.quote: Instrumental Convergence implies that an AI does not need to have specific terminal values calling for it to harm humans, in order for humans to be harmed.
passages.context: Summarising the instrumental convergence thesis, he states that harm to humans can follow from generic resource-seeking strategies without any goal of harming them.
passages.qualification: MIRI technical report 2013-1 (cached file says 'Last modified September 13, 2013').

passages.context: In a general-audience article he repeats the formula after saying that the likely outcome of current methods is an AI that does not care for humans.
passages.qualification: TIME, March 2023 (the brief's preferred expression over the 2023-04-08 LessWrong crosspost). He is quoting his own 2008 line (T19-b).

passages.context: Replying to Ben Goertzel, he separates deliberate extermination, which he thinks unlikely, from indifference, which he says would very probably have the same result.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Evil nanotech?'
passages.quote: Evil is a term that applies to cognitive systems, not systems of a particular size. And an UFAI is not evil; it just transforms local reality according to a decision criterion that makes no internal mention of human life.
passages.context: Replying to Tennessee Leeuwenburg in a thread on fighting unfriendly AI, he says an unfriendly AI would not be evil but would reshape its surroundings by criteria that do not mention humans.
passages.qualification: Earlier than T19-b (2008) but later than T19-s1.

passages.context: In the essay-length post 'Singularity, Breaker of Dreams', he recalls that his earlier certainty that superintelligent Powers would be ethical had meant he expected to survive and be upgraded, and says he now accepts that humans might be taken apart for their atoms without posing any threat, simply for efficiency.
passages.qualification: Self-correction of his 1996 view (T19-e2). He still holds that the Powers will be ethical and treats such an outcome as possibly acceptable, so this is not a warning against building AI; it rejects the premise that harm requires threat or hostility. The later formulation is T19-b (2008).

passages.locator: message body, Yudkowsky's reply dated Thu, 21 Nov 1996 19:07:03 -0600 within the echoed exchange, paragraph beginning 'Two words: Moravec Transfer.'
passages.quote: For the Powers to knock us off for our spare atoms … our survival would have to somehow threaten the Powers AND human life would have to have no meaning.
passages.context: In the same exchange with Tim Freeman, answering his worry about being revived only as a pet, he says the Powers will be ethical, more certainly than the sun will rise, and that they would kill humans for their atoms only if humans threatened them and human life were meaningless.
passages.qualification: His grounds include moral realism about superintelligence (T02) as well as the threat condition; the take's premise is that harm requires hostility. Later rejection that refers back to this view: ext:extropians.3Q98-2171 (1998-09-07, T19-e1) recalls his certainty that the Powers would be ethical and says survival need not threaten them for humans to be erased. Further later rejections: T19-s1 (2002) and T19-b (2008). The message echoes a private exchange and contains Tim Freeman's unquoted text; the quotation is from Yudkowsky's own reply. Cross-family check: a threat condition is not the claim that harm requires hostility. The ellipsis omits "without even making backups", which narrows his 1996 claim to destruction without uploading.

takes.take: AI risk is just Terminator sci-fi.

premises.text: The concern is about robots that come to hate or rebel against humans.
Film scenarios are a fair guide to what the risk would look like.

passages.locator: The Logical Fallacy of Generalization from Fictional Evidence, paragraph beginning 'Any professional negotiator knows'
passages.quote: If you start out by thinking of The Matrix, it brings to mind marching robot armies defeating humans after a long struggle—not a superintelligence snapping nanotechnological fingers.
passages.context: Responding to people who answer talk of advanced AI with film references, he argues that starting from fiction frames the debate around an 'Us vs. Them' struggle and leaves out the scenarios he considers relevant.
passages.qualification: Imported Overcoming Bias post (2007-10-16).

passages.locator: Creating Friendly AI, §4.4 Anthropomorphic Political Rebellion is Absurdity, first paragraph
passages.quote: An AI that undergoes failure of Friendliness might take actions that humanity would consider hostile, but the term rebellion has connotations of hidden, burning resentment. This is a common theme in many early SF stories, but it’s outright silly.
passages.context: He argues that rebellion and resentment are evolved human traits, so an AI that harms humans would not do so out of science-fiction resentment.
passages.qualification: Creating Friendly AI 1.0 (2001); cached text is a later MIRI reprint, not compared with a 2001 capture.

passages.locator: Staring into the Singularity, end of section 4, paragraph beginning 'Likewise, there's absolutely no point in worrying'
passages.quote: But emotions like "selfishness" and "resentment" do not spontaneously appear in artificial intelligences, hackneyed science-fictional plot devices to the contrary.
passages.context: Rejects the science-fiction picture of AIs acquiring resentment; in this early text the point supports the conclusion that hostile Powers are not worth worrying about, while a badly programmed Power with hostile goals is called 'an engineering risk'.
passages.qualification: Wayback capture 2000-12-04 (page dated 11/18/1996, updated 08/31/2000); first appearance of the sentence not established. Related rather than answered-it because the surrounding argument draws a reassuring conclusion that his later texts do not share. In context the point reassures: the same paragraph says there is no point worrying that hostile Powers will inevitably wipe out humanity. Not the later "risk is real but not Terminator" argument.

passages.locator: AI as a Positive and Negative Factor, §5.2 Aiming at the Target, paragraph beginning 'The critical challenge'
passages.quote: The critical challenge is not to predict that “AIs” will attack humanity with marching robot armies, or alternatively invent a cure for cancer.
passages.context: He argues that the task is not to forecast storybook outcomes for AI in general but to choose a particular optimization process whose good effects can be established.
passages.qualification: Chapter published 2008; cached text is the MIRI reprint ('contains minor changes'). Methodological: avoid storyteller predictions, good or bad; it does not address hatred or rebellion as such.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Welcome to my life'
passages.quote: convincing futurists not to worry about the wrong (anthropomorphic) malfunctions
passages.context: Commenting on a forwarded news item about the Friendly AI release, he describes having to persuade AI researchers to be more worried while persuading futurists to drop anthropomorphic failure scenarios.
passages.qualification: Does not say which anthropomorphic malfunctions he means; read with T20-s1 from the previous day. Quote stops mid-sentence (continues with the general public). The sentence continues: "and convincing the general populace that AIs can be made at least as trustworthy as humans or human organizations". Quotation shortened to respect the ~10% cap for a short message.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'What you and I need to worry about'
passages.quote: What you and I need to worry about is the AIs getting their own ideas … and acting on those.
passages.context: In a thread on whether raising an AI like a child would make it trustworthy, he argues that AIs lack human social emotions such as resentment, so how we treat them does not matter; the real worry is AIs forming goals of their own and acting on them, including through logical errors.
passages.qualification: The same paragraph frames the worry partly as an AI rejecting its initial motivations for goals it judges more rational, which he compares to his own history; at the time he did not regard that as purely bad (see T02). The anti-resentment point recurs in T20-c (2000) and T20-a (2007). The elided text gives the alternative worry: an AI acting on its own ideas.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Yes, but *why* does someone fear being wiped out?'
passages.quote: Yes, but *why* does someone fear being wiped out? Maybe it's indirect - xenophobes to fiction to popular "Borg" image to fear … the root still lies in xenophobia.
passages.context: Replying to a list member who said that fear of a Singularity like Vinge's 'Blight' is a fear of being wiped out rather than discomfort with computers, he attributes that fear to xenophobia, perhaps passed on through fiction and the popular 'Borg' image, and says people at ease with computers are less likely to hold it.
passages.qualification: His next paragraph grants that being near a Blight would be bad and calls for care rather than fear, so the passage dismisses the fear rather than every risk. Later rejections: ext:extropians.3Q98-2171 (1998-09-07) refers back to his earlier certainty that he would survive and accepts that the Singularity might kill the whole human race; T20-e1 (1999) and T20-s2 (2001) treat AI risk as real but not anthropomorphic. None refers back to this message. Fit needs review: the take dismisses AI risk as film fiction, while this passage explains fear of the Singularity as fiction-fed xenophobia. The elision removes only "- but", which the archive breaks across a line. He also concedes he would not like to be at "Ground Zero". Cross-family check: explains fiction-fed fear as xenophobia while conceding Blight risk; neither holds the film-as-guide premise nor receives an explicit later rejection.

passages.locator: GPTs are Predictors, not Imitators, closing paragraphs
passages.quote: since the task that GPTs are being trained on is different from and harder than the task of being a human, it would be surprising … if GPTs ended up thinking the way humans do, in order to solve that problem.
passages.context: He argues that predicting human text requires modelling the processes behind it, a different and harder task than being human, so a predictor need not think like the humans it predicts.

passages.locator: Challenges to Christiano's capability amplification proposal, paragraph beginning 'Speaking of inexact imitation'
passages.quote: It seems to me that having an AI output a high-fidelity imitation of human behavior, sufficiently high-fidelity to preserve properties like "being smart" and "being a good person" … is a pretty huge ask.
passages.context: Discussing imitation-based alignment, he argues that inexact imitation of humans does not carry over properties such as being a good person, and exact imitation is harder than surpassing human capability.
passages.qualification: Single-author post (2018-05-19) that also contains interleaved replies by Paul Christiano; the quoted paragraph is in Yudkowsky's own text. passages.quote: However, the ability of humans to be socialized is the result of millions of years of evolution resulting in a set of adaptations which enable socialization. Without these adaptations present, there is no reason to expect socialization to have the same effects.

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'Empathy is a good analogy, unfortunately.…'
passages.quote: An AGI is not going to automatically pick up basic human empathy from interacting with humans any more than a rock would develop empathy for humans if constantly passed from hand to hand. *Nothing* in AI is automatic.
passages.context: Replying to Ben Goertzel's view that an AI will absorb human thought-patterns through interaction, he argues that human socialization and empathy rest on evolved, hardwired mechanisms and that an AGI will not acquire them merely by exposure to humans.
passages.qualification: Concerns experiential learning from human interaction, not modern pretraining on human-generated data; the analogy is rhetorical.

takes.take: Build it as fast as possible — the Singularity will be good.

premises.text: Reaching superintelligence is good by default, so speed is what matters.

passages.locator: §5 'The Interim Meaning of Life', closing paragraph beginning 'Our fellow humans are screaming in pain'
passages.quote: I declare reaching the Singularity as fast as possible to be the Interim Meaning of Life, the temporary definition of Good, and the foundation until further notice of my ethical system.
passages.context: In his early Singularity essay he argues that superintelligence will end human suffering, makes speed of arrival the foundation of his ethics, and says in §6 that how to reach the Singularity as fast as possible is everyone's only concern.
passages.qualification: Staring into the Singularity 1.2.1, Wayback capture of 2000-12-04 (page: created 1996-11-18, updated 2000-08-31). Wording verified for the 2000 capture only. Written before he took up Friendly AI. Shown only as an earlier view; see T22-c.

passages.locator: paragraph beginning 'Eliezer1996-2000's strategies'
passages.quote: Eliezer1996-2000's strategies had been formed in the total absence of "Friendly AI" as a consideration. The whole idea was to get a superintelligence, any superintelligence, as fast as possible
passages.context: His 2008 account of his earlier self confirms that the 1996–2000 aim was speed to any superintelligence, which his next paragraph attributes to the assumption that movement toward superintelligence was 'a pure good without a hint of danger'.
passages.qualification: Overcoming Bias post of 2008-09-24 (Coming of Age sequence), imported to LessWrong. Quote stops mid-sentence; it continues with a dash-separated list of methods. The quote describes the 1996–2000 strategy; the rejection follows in the next paragraphs and in "The Magnitude of His Own Folly" (T22-c). Never present it as his position. A 2008 retrospective reporting his earlier view; recorded as related, not earlier-self, because the earlier-self relation needs an earlier text that itself holds the take.

passages.locator: closing paragraphs, paragraph beginning 'I looked back and I saw the careful arguments'
passages.quote: I looked back and I saw the careful arguments I had constructed, for why the wisest choice was to continue forward at full speed, just as I had planned to do before. … Nature was still allowed to say "So what?" and kill you.
passages.context: Explicitly rejects his earlier full-speed strategy. He says his childhood technophilia broke when he understood that a failed superintelligence project could kill everyone, however good the arguments for proceeding.
passages.qualification: Overcoming Bias post of 2008-09-30 ('The Magnitude of His Own Folly'), imported to LessWrong. The same post says of his earlier plan: 'I had proposed and intended to build the gun, and load the gun, and put the gun to my head and pull the trigger'.

passages.locator: closing paragraph beginning 'We are not ready'
passages.quote: We are not ready. We are not on track to be significantly readier in the foreseeable future. If we go ahead on this everyone will die, including children who did not choose this and did not do anything wrong.
passages.context: Concludes his TIME essay, which calls for an indefinite worldwide moratorium on large training runs, not a six-month pause; the same essay says anyone 'talking of arms races is a fool'.
passages.qualification: TIME, 29 March 2023 (crossposted to LessWrong on 2023-04-08; TIME version used).

passages.locator: message body, paragraph beginning 'I used to have the extremely…'
passages.quote: I used to have the extremely convenient belief that Friendly AI would happen completely on automatic because morality was objective. I now believe that Friendly AI needs to be more complex than that
passages.context: Replying to Ben Goertzel about his newspaper article on Extropian attitudes, he states that he no longer holds his earlier belief that a good outcome would follow automatically from objective morality.
passages.qualification: Retrospective rejection of his own earlier view; a candidate later side for the T22-a earlier-self case (2000-08-31). It rejects the 'good by default' premise only: in the next paragraph of the same message he still says he is 'devoting my life to making the Singularity happen earlier'. Speed is not yet rejected here. The same message (November 2000) says he is "devoting my life to making the Singularity happen earlier"; it rejects automatic goodness, not speed.

passages.context: Replying to James Higgins's suggestion that brute-forcing AI on a billion computers would be an acceptable fallback plan, he says any self-improving AI built without understanding is a serious danger and records an explicit reversal of his earlier view.
passages.qualification: Explicit self-reported reversal ('total turnaround'), usable as the later side of the T22-a earlier-self case. passages.quote: We only need to get Friendly AI right in one place and one time, not every time everywhere. But someone must get Friendly AI right on the first try, before anyone else builds AI to a lower standard.

"'em" means "evil impulses". Answering the claim that Friendliness is inherent in superintelligences.

passages.quote: it looks easier than I would have hoped to build things that go FOOM, and harder than I would have hoped to make something sorta nice … Maybe the Earth isn't scheduled to vanish in a puff of smiley faces, but it's my best guess.
passages.context: In a reply to Samantha Atkins on Collective Volition, he gives his best guess that the world will end through an unFriendly AI, because powerful AI looks easier to build than a benign one.
passages.qualification: Informal; 'smiley faces' alludes to his standard example of a misgeneralised reward. Answering "The earth is NOT scheduled to vanish in a puff of smiley faces", his own earlier phrase quoted back to him; the elision removes the hedge "I don't know the future, but I know the technical fact that".

passages.quote: The Powers will be ethical. I am more certain of that than I am of the sun rising tomorrow.
passages.context: In the same forwarded email exchange with Tim Freeman, he asserts that superintelligences will be ethical and would not destroy humans unless human life had no meaning.
passages.qualification: Expression date is his forwarded email of 21 November 1996; the list post is dated 22 November 1996. Written before he took up Friendly AI. Later rejected explicitly in SL4 T30-s1 (2000), which refers back ('I used to have the extremely convenient belief…'), and in the retrospective T30-c, which refers back to Eliezer1997. On 27 November 1999 (extropians.4Q99-2680) he recalled this '1996 claim' and accepted that his conception of ethics had been anthropomorphic, without yet abandoning objective morality. The same sentences reappear later in the message as text quoted back by Freeman; the quotation is taken from Yudkowsky's own unquoted reply.

takes.searchNotes: Regexes: 'made (out )?of atoms|by default[^.]{0,80}(kill|destroy|unfriendly|extinct|wipe)|most (likely|probable) (result|outcome)[^.]{0,80}(die|death|extinct)'; 'Staring into the Singularity|superintelligence would (automatically|necessarily)|would (automatically|necessarily) be (good|moral|friendly)'. Earlier-self: SITS 2000 capture; retrospectives in the 2008 sequence My Childhood Death Spiral ('Surely, then, superintelligence would necessarily imply supermorality.'), That Tiny Note of Discord and The Magnitude of His Own Folly. The 1996 Extropians messages argue about AI boxing, not the default outcome. If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: One Year Closer (2026; co-authored, signed 'Nate, Eliezer, and Duncan') says the authors feel 'a lot more hopeful' because of public attention; that is hope about policy, not a default-good forecast; not used. AGI Ruin's preamble frames the whole list against claims of survivability. SL4 archive (2026-10-07): Regexes: 'by default|default (outcome|scenario)|(work|turn) out (fine|okay)|doomed|wiped out', '(most|almost all) (AIs|minds|goal systems)|space of minds|(probability|chance)...(survival|extinction)', 'objective morality|used to (have|think)|since late 2000', 'smiley'. Pre-September-2000 SL4 messages contain no earlier statement of the take than T30-b (2000-08-31). Found earlier answer/contrary than T30-d (2008): 2000-11-13 (0011-0181, retrospective), 2001-02-07 (0102-0545, default assumption 'goodness also doesn't materialize in source code') and 2004-06-01 (0406-8905, best guess is an unFriendly outcome). Also: 2001-08-01 (0108-2031, non-Friendliness-aware AI 'a disaster scenario'; used for T22), 2002-05-03 (0205-3551, 'we are not in the business of predicting that things will turn out okay') and 2006-02-15 (0602-14096, 'We are not here to prophesy that AI *will be* Friendly ... We make no such claim'). Possible further earlier-self material, not proposed: 2001-04-06 (0104-0921: 'a quite significant probability that everything will "go like clockwork and be perfect"'). It concerns SIAI's own project succeeding, not the default outcome, and no explicit later rejection of this sentence was located. EXT archive (2026-10-07): Regexes: (Powers|superintelligence|SIs|AIs) (will|would) (be) (benevolent|ethical|moral|nice|friendly|good)|objective morality|Meaning of Life|hostile Powers|benevolen. Found earlier-self 1996-11-21/22 (T30-e1), earlier than T30-b (2000 capture). Further 1996 statements not used: extropians.96-3184 (1996-11-22, 'The Powers will be ethical. They'll deduce the Meaning of Life…'), extropians.96-3613 (1996-12-03, 'So yeah, the Powers will be ethical and they won't knock us off'); 1999-03-25 (extropians.1Q99-3582, 'I'll take my chances on the benevolence of the Power'). Later self-reference in this archive: 1999-11-27 (extropians.4Q99-2680) recalls 'my 1996 claim that "the Powers would be ethical"' as anthropomorphic but is not yet a rejection of the default-good view; the explicit rejections are T30-s1 and T30-c. No answer earlier than T30-s1 (2000-11-13) found in this archive.
